note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Operate in an autonomous team environment

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is an autonomous (self-managed) work team?
options: A team that works with no rules, targets or safety checks at all
A team where one supervisor hands out every task to each member
A team that plans, shares out and checks its own work within limits
A team in which each person works alone on a separate job

questions.stem: Your self-managed team may decide its own order of work. Which decision should still go to the manager?
options: Buying a new welding machine outside the agreed budget
Who welds and who fits up the frames on Tuesday morning
Which of today's gates to start on first
When to take the tea break within the shift

questions.stem: Which team target is written well?
options: Work hard this week and make good, strong welds on every job
Make as many grills as we can, as soon as we possibly can
Try our best to keep every customer happy with the work
Finish and inspect 12 window grills by Friday at 3 p.m.

questions.stem: Why should the whole team help set its weekly targets, rather than only the team leader?
options: So that no one can be blamed if a target is missed
Members are more committed to targets they helped to set
So the targets can be set lower and finished easily
Because the manager is not allowed to set any of the targets

questions.stem: When a team shares out the tasks for a balcony-rail job, what should decide who does each task?
options: Who arrived at the workshop first that morning
Who has worked for the company the longest
Skills, qualifications, safety and a fair share of work
Who is the closest friend of the team leader

questions.stem: Only one member of the team is qualified to weld the coded joints on a job. What is the main risk for the team?
options: If she is absent, that part of the job stops
She will become too tired to weld well by noon
The others will forget how to weld altogether
The client will refuse to pay for her extra skill

questions.stem: Why do autonomous teams rotate jobs, such as cutting, fitting and welding, among the members?
options: So that nobody becomes very good at any one task
So the work takes longer and earns more overtime
So the team leader does not need to plan any work
So more members can cover each task when needed

questions.stem: Kadeem wants to learn TIG welding, but the team is behind on a job. What is the best plan?
options: Let him learn on the customer's stainless rails right away
Agree a time for a skilled member to train him once on track
Tell him TIG welding is not his job and never will be
Let him practise alone, without anyone watching, at lunch time

questions.stem: When is consensus (everyone agreeing to support a decision) the best way for a team to decide?
options: When someone may be hurt and action is needed at once
When the question is about a legal or safety rule
When there is time and everyone must back the choice
When the matter is very small and nobody minds

questions.stem: A fire starts in the bay while the team is discussing its work plan. How should the decision on what to do be made?
options: The nearest trained person acts at once, as the emergency plan says
The team holds a quick vote, then follows the majority view
The team waits for the manager to arrive and decide what to do
Everyone gives an opinion first, so that nobody is left out

questions.stem: The team cannot agree whether to tack the frames on the bench or on a floor jig. Both ways are safe. What is a fair way to settle it?
options: Let the loudest member choose, to save time
Toss a coin and use that way for every job
Ask the client which way the team should work
Try both on one frame, compare, then choose

questions.stem: A team keeps finding porosity in its MIG welds. What is the best first step in solving it as a team?
options: Change every gas cylinder in the shop at once
Collect facts: when, where and on which machine
Find out which welder is to blame and warn him
Turn the voltage up on every machine in the bay

questions.stem: What is the purpose of asking "Why?" several times in a row (the 5 Whys) about a problem?
options: To find out which member caused the problem
To make the meeting last long enough to be useful
To get past the symptom to the root cause
To show the manager that the team is working hard

questions.stem: A team draws a fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram for gates being delivered late. What does it help the team do?
options: Sort possible causes under headings like people, methods and materials
Draw the outline of each gate to the right scale for the client
Show the quickest delivery route to each customer's house
Work out the price of each gate for the final invoice

questions.stem: In the Plan–Do–Check–Act cycle, what happens at the "Check" stage?
options: The team plans what change it will try
The team carries out the change on the job
The team makes the change the new standard way of working
The team measures whether the change worked

questions.stem: A trial of a new fit-up jig cut the time to tack a frame by 20%. What should the team do next?
options: Stop using the jig, because the trial is now over
Write it into the method and train every member
Keep the jig hidden so other teams cannot use it
Use it only when the team leader is watching

questions.stem: Which is the most useful measure of the quality of a fabrication team's work?
options: The hours the team spent on site each week
The number of electrodes bought each month
The number of welds rejected at inspection
How many members came to the weekly meeting

questions.stem: A board on the workshop wall shows each day's target and actual output. Why is it useful to a self-managed team?
options: Everyone can see at once if the team is on track
The manager can see which member to punish for a bad day
Visitors can see how busy the workshop has been
It replaces the need to inspect any of the work

questions.stem: The team's output fell by a third this week. Before deciding what to do, what should the team look at?
options: Which member to blame, so that he can be warned
How to work longer hours until the gap is closed
Whether the target should simply be cut by a third
The causes, such as absence, breakdowns or rework

questions.stem: One member is overloaded while another is waiting for material to arrive. What should the team do?
options: Leave things as they are, because each has his own job
Move the waiting member to help, if he can do it safely
Send the waiting member home without pay for the day
Tell the busy member to work faster and skip his breaks

questions.stem: A member phones in sick on the day of a site installation in Spanish Town. What should the team do first?
options: Cancel the installation without telling the client
Carry on with one person less and skip the checks
Review the plan and share out the work safely
Ask a passer-by on site to help lift the gate

questions.stem: In a self-managed team, who is responsible for the quality of each weld?
options: The welder first, and then the team as a whole
Only the inspector, at the end of the job
Only the team leader, who signs off the job card
Only the customer, once the job is delivered

questions.stem: A member often leaves early, and others finish his work. What should the team do first?
options: Complain about him to the manager behind his back
Leave his share undone so that the manager notices
Stop speaking to him until he changes his ways
Talk to him privately, with facts, and agree a change

questions.stem: Why do team members check each other's work, such as a frame's diagonals before it is welded?
options: So that the person who made a mistake can be named
A second person catches errors before they cost more
So the inspector at the end has less work to do
So that each member's work takes twice as long

questions.stem: A new team is arguing about roles and ways of working. Which stage of team development is this usually called?
options: Forming
Norming
Storming
Performing

questions.stem: What usually shows that a team has reached the performing stage?
options: Members work well together with little supervision
Members still argue about who does each task
Members are polite but unsure of their roles
Members wait to be told what to do each hour

questions.stem: A new member joins the team halfway through a job. What is the best way to bring him in?
options: Give him the hardest task so he proves himself
Let him watch from the side until the job ends
Hand him the job file and let him work it out
Pair him with an experienced member at first

questions.stem: In a self-managed team, who may stop a job that looks unsafe?
options: Only the manager or owner
Any member who sees the danger
Only the Centre's safety officer
Only the elected team leader

questions.stem: The team wants to finish early by skipping the fire watch after hot work. What should a Level 3 member do?
options: Agree, as long as everyone leaves the bay together
Agree, but leave a fire extinguisher beside the job
Refuse, explain the risk and keep the fire watch
Say nothing, as the team has already voted on it

questions.stem: Tension is growing because one member always seems to get the easy jobs. What should the team do?
options: Agree an open way of sharing tasks and review it weekly
Give that member all the hardest jobs for a month
Ignore it, as the tension will settle down by itself
Let each member choose any task he likes each day

questions.stem: A member keeps making jokes about a co-worker's accent and home parish. What should the others do?
options: Laugh along so that the team stays relaxed
Ignore it, because it is only a joke between workmates
Tell the co-worker to ignore it and work on
Say it is not acceptable, and report it if it goes on

questions.stem: Your team needs the overhead crane, which the maintenance team is also using today. What is the best way to settle it?
options: Use the crane while the other team is at lunch
Agree times for each team with the other leader
Ask the manager to ban the other team from using it
Lift the load by hand to avoid any argument

questions.stem: Why does a self-managed team still report its progress to the manager?
options: So the manager can do the team's planning for it
Because the team is not trusted to do the work
So the business can plan and promise work to clients
So the manager can share out each member's tasks

questions.stem: A self-managed team runs out of grinding discs every Thursday. What is the best fix?
options: Track how many are used each week and set a re-order level
Borrow discs from another team every Thursday afternoon
Stop all grinding work on Thursdays and on Fridays
Keep using worn-out discs until the new stock arrives

questions.stem: Why should a team's daily start-up meeting be short and held standing at the work area?
options: So that members cannot ask any questions
So the team leader can do all the talking
So that minutes are not needed for the meeting
It keeps the meeting on today's tasks and problems

questions.stem: A trainee suggests a cheaper way to make gate hinges. What should the team do?
options: Tell her to wait until she has more experience first
Listen, test it safely and thank her for the idea
Use it on the next customer job without a trial
Pass it to the manager and forget all about it

questions.stem: The team finds that a batch of brackets sent out last week has its holes in the wrong place. What should it do first?
options: Wait to see whether the client notices the mistake
Make a new batch quietly and swap them at night
Tell the manager and the client, and agree a fix
Find out who drilled them and dock his pay

questions.stem: The team agreed to finish a staircase by Thursday, but a crane delay means it will be Friday. When should the client be told?
options: As soon as the team knows about the delay
On Thursday evening, when the job is not done
On Friday, once the staircase is finished
Only if the client phones to ask about it

questions.stem: At the end of a job the team holds a review. Which question is the most useful one to ask?
options: Who made the most mistakes on this job?
How can we get the next job finished faster than this one?
Was the manager pleased with the team's work?
What worked, what did not, and what will we change?

questions.stem: What is a good way for a team to recognise good work by a member?
options: Say nothing, as good work is simply expected
Thank them in front of the team for the specific work
Give them the easy jobs for the rest of the year
Tell them privately that they are the favourite

questions.stem: Why is keeping the team's work area tidy a shared duty, rather than one person's job?
options: The cleaner will not come in while the team is working
It gives members something to do when work is slow
Everyone uses it, and clutter causes trips and delays
The manager judges the team only on how tidy it is

questions.stem: A member finishes her task early. In a self-managed team, what should she do?
options: Check the board or ask the team which task to take next
Wait at her bench until the team leader gives her more work
Go home early, since her own task is now finished
Start any job she likes, without telling the others

questions.stem: Why should a team write down its ground rules, such as start times and phone use at work?
options: So the rules can be changed each day without notice
So the team leader can make up rules as he goes
So the manager does not need to speak to the team
So everyone knows what is expected of them

questions.stem: What does a team skills matrix show?
options: The pay rate of each member of the team
Who can do each task, and who needs training
The order in which the jobs must be done
The tools each member has signed out today

questions.stem: Halfway through a job, the team finds a drawing error that will make a frame 50 mm too short. What should the team do?
options: Make it to the drawing, as the error is not the team's fault
Make it 50 mm longer and say nothing to anyone about it
Stop that part, tell the designer and agree the change first
Scrap the frame and start the whole job again from new

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What one word names the first stage of team development, when members have just met and are polite but unsure of their roles?
What do we call a level of output agreed in advance that the team aims to reach, such as 40 brackets a day?
In the PDCA cycle (Plan, Do, Check, ...), what word does the letter A stand for?
What do we call the cause at the bottom of a problem which, once fixed, stops the problem coming back?
What name is given to training each worker to do several different jobs in the team?
What do we call the way of deciding in which the choice with the most votes is taken?
A fishbone diagram is also named after the Japanese engineer who made it popular. What is that name?
What Japanese word is used for continuous improvement made in small steps by everyone?
The 5S method starts with "Sort". What is the second S, which means giving everything its set place?
A team's target is 40 brackets a day. It made 36. What percentage of the target did it reach?
What do we call the written record of a meeting, listing the decisions and the actions agreed?
What is the name of the written document in which a team sets out its purpose, goals, roles and ground rules?
What do we call an experienced worker who is paired with a new member to guide him through his first weeks?
What word names the extra work needed to put right a job that failed inspection?
What word describes a member's duty to answer for his own work and its results?

essays.stem: Explain what an autonomous (self-managed) team is, how it differs from a team that is closely supervised, and the benefits and limits of working this way in a fabrication shop.
essays.modelAnswer: An autonomous team is given a goal, such as a batch of gates by a set date, and then plans, shares out, carries out and checks the work itself. In a closely supervised team, a supervisor decides each person's tasks and checks each step. In a self-managed team the members agree the order of work, decide who does what, solve day-to-day problems and track their own output and quality. The benefits are faster decisions on the shop floor, more skills in the team because members rotate tasks, more commitment because people own the targets, and more ideas for improvement. The limits are that the team still works inside rules set by the business: safety rules, the budget, the specification and the law. Big decisions, such as buying equipment, changing a price or a delivery date, or dealing with discipline, go to the manager. It also needs members who are willing to take responsibility and who report honestly.
markingPoints: Defines it: the team plans, shares out, does and checks its own work towards an agreed goal
Contrasts it with a supervised team, where a supervisor gives tasks and checks each step
Gives benefits: faster decisions, wider skills, commitment, improvement ideas
Gives limits: works within safety rules, budget, specification and law; big decisions go to the manager
Notes it needs members who take responsibility and report honestly

essays.stem: Your team of five has one week to make 20 window grills and fit them at a school in Mandeville. Explain how the team would share out the work and keep track of it during the week.
essays.modelAnswer: First the team reads the job card and drawing together and breaks the job into tasks: checking materials, marking out and cutting, fitting and tacking, welding, cleaning and painting, loading and fitting on site. Using the team's skills matrix, we match people to tasks, making sure that qualified members do the welding and site work, and that one member is learning each task alongside someone experienced. We agree a simple daily plan and put it on a board, with targets for each day, for example four grills cut and tacked on Monday. Each morning we hold a short stand-up meeting to check yesterday's output against the plan, raise problems and move people if one task is falling behind. We check each other's work, such as the sizes of the first grill, before the rest are made. If the week's target is at risk, we tell the manager early. At the end we record the actual hours and any lessons for the next job.
markingPoints: Breaks the job into tasks from the job card and drawing
Uses a skills matrix to match people to tasks, with training built in
Sets daily targets on a visible board
Holds short daily meetings to check progress and move people where needed
Checks work (first-off), tells the manager early of risks, records hours and lessons

essays.stem: Many of the steel gates your team makes are twisted after welding. Explain how the team could use a problem-solving method, such as the 5 Whys or a fishbone diagram with Plan–Do–Check–Act, to fix the problem for good.
essays.modelAnswer: First the team states the problem clearly with facts: for example, 6 of the last 15 gates were twisted by more than the 3 mm allowed. We collect data on each gate: who made it, which jig or bench was used, the welding sequence and the material. Then we draw a fishbone diagram with headings such as people, methods, materials and equipment, and list every possible cause. For the most likely causes we ask "why?" several times. For example, the gates twist because the welds are made all on one side first; that happens because there is no written welding sequence; and that is because the method was never agreed. Next we plan a change, such as a clamping jig and a balanced welding sequence, and try it on a few gates. We check the results by measuring twist on each gate. If it worked, we act: write it into the method, train everyone and keep measuring.
markingPoints: States the problem with facts and collects data
Uses a fishbone diagram to list possible causes under headings
Uses repeated "why?" questions to reach the root cause
Plans and trials a change (Plan and Do), then measures the result (Check)
Makes the change standard and trains everyone (Act)

essays.stem: Describe the usual stages a new team goes through as it develops, and explain what a Level 3 member can do to help the team through each one.
essays.modelAnswer: In the forming stage, members are new to each other and polite but unsure of their roles. A Level 3 member can help by making sure the goal, the rules and each person's role are clear. In the storming stage, people start to disagree about how the work should be done and who does what. The Level 3 member helps by keeping arguments on the facts, listening to each side and agreeing fair ways of working. In the norming stage, the team settles on its ways of working and members start to trust each other. Here the Level 3 member helps write down the agreed methods and ground rules and encourages people to share skills. In the performing stage, the team works well with little supervision, solves its own problems and meets its targets. The Level 3 member keeps it there by recognising good work, bringing in improvements and helping new members fit in, since a change of members can send a team back a stage.
markingPoints: Forming: new and unsure; help by making goals, rules and roles clear
Storming: disagreements; help by keeping to facts, listening and agreeing fair methods
Norming: agreed ways and growing trust; help by writing down methods and sharing skills
Performing: works well with little supervision; help by recognition and improvement
Notes that a change of members can send the team back a stage

essays.stem: One member's time-keeping and work have been slipping for two weeks, and the rest of the team is unhappy. Explain how the team should deal with this fairly.
essays.modelAnswer: The team should not gossip, freeze the member out or leave his work undone to make a point. First, one member, usually the team leader or a member he trusts, should speak to him privately, as soon as possible. The talk should be about facts, not feelings: for example, "You arrived after 8:00 on six days, and two of your frames failed the diagonal check." He should be given the chance to explain, because there may be a reason such as illness, a family problem or not understanding a task. Together they agree what will change, any help the team can give, such as coaching or a change of task, and when they will review it. The agreement is noted. If things improve, this should be recognised. If they do not improve, or if the problem is serious, such as safety or honesty, it goes to the manager, because discipline is outside the team's authority.
markingPoints: Deals with it directly and privately, not through gossip or freezing him out
Uses facts, not feelings or labels
Listens to his side; looks for causes and offers help
Agrees changes and a review date, and notes the agreement
Refers to the manager if there is no improvement or it is serious (discipline is outside the team's authority)

essays.stem: Explain how a self-managed team knows which decisions it can make itself and which must go to management. Give at least two examples of each.
essays.modelAnswer: The limits should be agreed with the manager when the team is set up and written in the team's charter or job instructions. In general, the team decides how to do the work it has been given, within the plan, budget, specification and safety rules. Examples are the order in which the day's tasks are done, who does which task, how to share the work when someone is absent, small improvements to methods and jigs, and housekeeping. Decisions that affect the business, the client or the law go to management. Examples are changing the price, the delivery date or the design agreed with the client, spending outside the budget, such as buying a new machine, hiring or disciplining staff, and accepting work that does not meet the specification. Safety rules can never be relaxed by the team. When the team is unsure where a decision falls, it should ask before acting, and it should report its decisions so that the manager is kept informed.
markingPoints: Limits are agreed with the manager and written down
Team decides how to do its work within the plan, budget, specification and safety rules
Gives at least two correct examples of team decisions
Gives at least two correct examples of management decisions (price, date, design, spending, staff, accepting non-conforming work)
Safety rules are never relaxed; asks when unsure and keeps the manager informed

essays.stem: Explain how a self-managed team makes safety a shared responsibility, rather than leaving it to one person.
essays.modelAnswer: In a self-managed team there may be no supervisor watching every task, so each member must look after his own safety and that of others. The team agrees that any member can stop a job that looks unsafe, without blame, and that safety comes before targets. Before each job, the team looks at the hazards together, for example hot work, lifting and grinding, and agrees the controls, such as screens, a fire watch, PPE and safe lifting. Members check each other's set-up and PPE and speak up politely if something is wrong. Safety tasks, such as checking extinguishers, the first-aid box and leads, are shared out on a rota, and done. Near misses and hazards are reported and discussed at the daily meeting so that the team can fix the cause. New members are briefed on the rules. Safety is one of the team's measures, so it is reviewed like output and quality.
markingPoints: Each member is responsible for himself and others
Any member can stop an unsafe job; safety comes before targets
The team assesses hazards and agrees controls before work
Members check each other; safety tasks are shared on a rota
Near misses are reported and discussed; safety is measured and reviewed

essays.stem: A new welder joins your team in the middle of a two-week job. Describe how the team would bring him in and support him.
essays.modelAnswer: Before he starts work, the team leader or his buddy makes sure he has had the Centre's or company's safety induction. Then he is shown round the work area: the exits, fire extinguishers, first-aid box, machines and stores. He is told the team's goal, the plan and the targets, and the ground rules, such as start times and phone use. He is introduced to each member and told who to ask about what. He is paired with an experienced buddy for the first days. His skills are checked against the skills matrix, for example with a test weld, before he is given a task that suits his skills and qualifications. He takes part in the daily meeting from the first day so that he feels part of the team. His buddy checks his work and gives friendly feedback. After a week, the team leader talks to him about how he is settling in and what training he needs, and updates the skills matrix.
markingPoints: Safety induction and a tour of the work area
Explains the goal, plan, targets and ground rules; introduces the members
Pairs him with an experienced buddy
Checks his skills before giving a suitable task; includes him in meetings
Gives feedback, reviews after a set time and updates the skills matrix

essays.stem: Explain how a fabrication team can measure its own performance. Choose three measures, and say how each is collected and how the team should use the results.
essays.modelAnswer: A team should measure a few things that it can control and that matter to the business. First, output against target: for example, the number of grills finished each day. This is collected by marking a board at the end of each shift. Second, quality: for example, the number of welds or items rejected at inspection each week. This comes from the inspection records. Third, safety: for example, the number of near misses reported and any injuries, from the near-miss book. Other measures could be the hours used against the hours planned, or material waste. The results should be shown on a board where everyone can see them, and looked at in the daily or weekly meeting. The team uses them to spot problems early, find causes and try improvements. The measures should never be used to blame one person, because that stops people reporting honestly. Trends over several weeks are more useful than one bad day.
markingPoints: Chooses measures the team controls that matter (output, quality, safety, hours or waste)
Explains how each measure is collected (board, inspection records, near-miss book)
Shows the results where everyone can see them
Reviews them in meetings to spot problems and drive improvement
Does not use them to blame individuals; looks at trends

essays.stem: Describe how your team would hold a review at the end of a job, and how it would turn the lessons into improvements.
essays.modelAnswer: The review should be held soon after the job, while people remember it, and should take about half an hour. Everyone who worked on the job takes part. Before the meeting, someone gathers the facts: planned and actual hours, materials used, inspection results, any rework, near misses and the client's comments. In the meeting, the team looks at three questions: what went well, what did not go well, and what we will change next time. The leader keeps the talk on the work and the methods, not on blaming people, and makes sure quieter members are heard. For each lesson, the team agrees an action, a person responsible and a date: for example, updating the cut list template, or making a jig. The notes are kept with the job file. At the start of the next similar job, the team reads the lessons from the last one and checks that the actions were done.
markingPoints: Holds the review soon after the job, with everyone involved
Gathers facts first (hours, materials, inspection, rework, client comments)
Asks what went well, what did not, and what to change; no blame
Agrees actions with a person and a date
Records the lessons and checks them at the start of the next job

practical1.title: Self-managed production of a batch of steel brackets, with a team plan, rotation of roles and a progress board
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a drawing and job card for a small batch of welded items that can be made at the Centre (for example eight angle-iron wall brackets with a gusset), the materials, and a time limit. The assessor does not tell the group who does what. As a self-managed team: (1) agree your ground rules and choose a team leader for the session; (2) break the job into tasks, fill in a simple skills matrix and share out the tasks so that each member does at least two different tasks (for example cutting and welding) and nobody works alone on a hazardous task; (3) draw a progress board with the target for each hour; (4) make the batch, with each member checking another member's work (for example the first bracket's sizes and squareness) before the rest are made; (5) update the board each hour and deal with any problem as a team; (6) inspect the finished batch, clean up and hold a 10-minute review that records what to change next time. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Drawing and job card for the batch (for example 8 brackets in 40 × 40 × 5 mm angle with 6 mm gussets)
Steel angle and flat bar for the batch, with a little spare
Cutting saw or grinder, marking-out tools, square and tape measure
Welding machine and consumables as the job card says
Flip-chart paper or whiteboard for the ground rules, skills matrix and progress board
photos: The ground rules, skills matrix and task list
The progress board at the start, with hourly targets
A member checking the first bracket against the drawing
Work in progress, showing members on different tasks
The progress board at the end, with actual output
The finished, inspected batch laid out
checklist: Took part in agreeing the ground rules and the sharing of tasks
Did at least two different tasks safely and to the drawing
Checked another member's work and gave clear, polite feedback
Updated the board or raised a problem with the team when it arose
Helped move people or change the plan when a task fell behind
Wore the right PPE and kept the work area safe and tidy
Gave at least one useful point in the review
safety: Wear the right PPE for each task: welding helmet and gloves, and safety glasses and face shield when cutting or grinding
Weld only in a booth or behind screens; warn others before striking an arc
Any member may stop a task that looks unsafe; the team then agrees a safe way before carrying on
Mark hot work and handle hot parts with tongs or pliers
Keep leads and offcuts off the walkways

practical2.title: Team problem-solving: find the cause of a quality problem, trial a fix and present the result
practical2.brief: The assessor sets the group a real quality problem with evidence, for example six small tack-welded frames that are out of square or twisted, a batch of parts with holes in the wrong place, or welds with porosity, together with the method the parts were made by. As a team: (1) state the problem in one sentence with measured facts, after measuring every part and recording the results on a data sheet; (2) draw a fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram of possible causes; (3) use the 5 Whys on the most likely cause; (4) plan a change (for example a simple jig, a clamping order or a better marking-out method) and agree who does what; (5) make two or three parts with the change and measure them in the same way; (6) compare before and after, and present your findings to the assessor in five minutes, with a written improvement sheet that says what should change in the method. Every member takes part in measuring, in the diagram and in the trial, and each presents one part of the findings. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Faulty parts and the method used to make them, from the assessor
Steel and consumables to make two or three trial parts
Measuring tools: tape, square, straight edge, feeler gauges or callipers as needed
Welding or drilling equipment as the trial needs, and clamps or scrap steel for a simple jig
Flip-chart paper, markers, data sheets and an improvement sheet
photos: The faulty parts being measured, with the data sheet
The 5 Whys worked through on paper
The change being trialled (for example the jig in use)
The before-and-after results and the improvement sheet
checklist: Measured parts accurately and recorded the results
Added sensible causes to the fishbone diagram
Took part in the 5 Whys and kept to facts, not blame
Did an agreed share of the trial safely
Measured the trial parts the same way as the faulty ones
Presented one part of the findings clearly
Listened to and built on other members' ideas
safety: Wear safety glasses and gloves when handling and measuring steel parts
Use full welding PPE and screens for any welding in the trial
Clamp work before drilling, and keep hands clear of the drill
Keep the work area tidy and clear of trip hazards
